title: Cleaning a Clock Movement
body:
Specifications

A full movement cleaning strips the movement to its plates, cleans every wheel, pinion, and pivot, and reassembles it with fresh oil. It is needed every five to ten years for a longcase clock, sooner in a dusty or damp house, and it is the single most effective maintenance a clock can receive.

Mechanism

Disassembly starts with letting down the power: weights are removed and held, or the mainspring is let down in a controlled way, and only then are the plates separated. Wheels are cleaned in clock cleaning solution, pivots are polished with pegwood and a pivot file, and the plates are brushed and rinsed. Reassembly reverses the order, with each wheel checked for freedom before the plates are closed.

Maintenance

Never clean a movement with the power still on, and never use household cleaners or water on a movement without drying it fully, because rust follows damp pivots. Keep the wheels in order as they come out, and photograph the movement before stripping it, so the order is certain on reassembly.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration cleaning also checks every pivot hole for wear, every tooth for damage, and every spring for set, and it replaces worn parts before reassembly rather than after. Test the movement on a stand for a week before returning it to its case.

Tools

Cleaning solution, pegwood, pivot files, screwdrivers, camera, and clock oil.

title: Oiling a Clock Movement
body:
Specifications

Oiling means placing one tiny drop of clock oil on each pivot and on each pallet face, and nowhere else. Clock oil is a light, non-gumming oil made for clock pivots, and it is used in far smaller amounts than most owners expect: a movement that looks wet has been over-oiled.

Mechanism

Oil is applied with a fine oiler to the pivot as it sits in its hole, so capillary action draws it in, and to the pallet impulse faces, where the escape wheel teeth slide. Oil on the teeth themselves, on the pendulum suspension, on the dial, or on the case does no good and attracts dust. Over-oiling is worse than slight under-oiling, because excess oil creeps onto the pendulum, the dial, and the escapement, and it carries dust into the pivots.

Maintenance

Oil only the points the maker specifies, one drop each, and never oil a clock that has not been cleaned, because new oil on old, dirty oil makes a grinding paste. Never use household oil, sewing-machine oil, or spray lubricants on a clock movement, because they gum or creep.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration oiling follows a full cleaning, with each pivot checked for freedom first, and the oil points are recorded in the service notes so the next service can see what was done. Test the rate for a week after oiling, because fresh oil changes the rate slightly.

Tools

Clock oil, fine oilers, loupe, pegwood, and service notes.

title: Setting a Clock in Beat
body:
Specifications

Beat setting means adjusting the crutch so the pendulum's tick sounds even on both sides, with equal intervals between ticks. A clock out of beat runs unevenly, loses power, and may stop, especially when it is level, and beat setting is the first correction to try before any other repair.

Mechanism

The pendulum hangs from its suspension, and the crutch fork pushes it through the anchor. If the crutch is bent slightly one way, the anchor releases one pallet early and the other late, so the ticks are uneven. Bending the crutch a fraction, or shifting the suspension, evens the ticks. The test is by ear or by a beat amplifier: the intervals left and right must match.

Maintenance

Set the beat with the clock level and in its case position, because a clock set in beat on a bench may be out of beat when hung on a wall that leans. Never bend the crutch by force against the anchor, and never bend the pendulum rod to set the beat.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration beat setting follows cleaning and levelling, and it is checked at full swing and at low swing, because a beat that is even at full swing can be uneven as the swing falls. Record the beat error in the service notes.

Tools

Beat amplifier, crutch bending tool, spirit level, and screwdrivers.

title: Bushing Worn Pivot Holes
body:
Specifications

Bushing means fitting a small brass bush into a pivot hole that has worn oval, so the pivot runs round and centred again. Pivot holes wear because the pivot turns in the hole under load for decades, and the wear is worst on the going train's lower wheels, which carry the most load.

Mechanism

The worn hole is reamed round and slightly larger, a brass bush is pressed or screwed in, and the bush is then reamed to fit the pivot with a small clearance, about two hundredths of a millimetre. The wheel must then sit at the correct depth with its neighbours, which is checked with a depthing tool before the plates are closed.

Maintenance

Check every pivot hole for wear before bushing, and bush only the holes that need it, because an unnecessary bush changes the wheel's position. Never bush a hole by hammering a bush in without reaming, because the plate cracks or the bush sits crooked.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration bushing uses bushes of the same brass as the plate, reams them to the pivot with a smooth finish, and checks the depthing of every wheel pair after bushing. Test the movement for freedom before oiling.

Tools

Bushing tool, reamers, brass bushes, depthing tool, and loupe.

title: Replacing a Suspension Spring
body:
Specifications

The suspension spring is the thin steel spring from which the pendulum hangs, and it sets the pendulum's effective length and its freedom to swing. It wears by flexing millions of times, and a cracked or kinked suspension makes the clock run unevenly or stop.

Mechanism

The pendulum hangs from the suspension spring's lower block, and the spring flexes as the pendulum swings, so the pendulum's pivot is the spring itself, with almost no friction. The spring's length and thickness set the pendulum's rate, and a spring that is too thick or too thin changes the rate and the swing. Replacement means fitting a spring of the same length and thickness, with its blocks square and its screws tight.

Maintenance

Handle a suspension spring by its blocks, never by the spring itself, because finger oil and bending weaken it. Check the spring for cracks under a loupe before fitting, and never straighten a kinked spring and reuse it, because it will crack at the kink.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration suspension uses a spring matched to the pendulum's weight, with the top block fixed firmly and the bottom block square to the rod. Test the swing for freedom and check the beat after fitting, because a new suspension often needs a beat adjustment.

Tools

Suspension springs, loupe, screwdrivers, and a beat tester.

title: Caring for a Clock Case
body:
Specifications

Case care means cleaning and protecting the wooden case, the brass fittings, and the glass, without damaging the finish or the movement inside. Longcase cases are usually mahogany, oak, or walnut, with brass hinges and a glazed door, and they suffer from sunlight, damp, and household polish more than from age.

Mechanism

Wood is cleaned with a soft, dry cloth, and only occasionally with a wax polish made for furniture, never with spray polish, which builds up and dulls the finish. Brass is cleaned with a soft cloth and, if needed, a gentle brass cleaner, kept away from the dial and the movement. Glass is cleaned with a soft cloth and a little glass cleaner, kept away from the dial's paint. The case must stand level, out of direct sunlight, and away from radiators and damp walls.

Maintenance

Never use water on a clock case, never spray polish near the dial, and never move a longcase clock with its weights and pendulum still in place, because the pendulum swings and the weights damage the case. Always remove the weights and pendulum before moving the case, even across a room.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration case repair matches the wood and finish, repairs veneer with matching veneer, and re-lacquers only the repaired area where possible, so the case keeps its age and character. Record the finish used, so future care matches it.

Tools

Soft cloths, furniture wax, brass cleaner, glass cleaner, and screwdrivers.

title: Movement Handling Safety
body:
Specifications

Movement handling safety covers the two real hazards in a clock: a wound mainspring that can unwind violently, and heavy driving weights that can fall. Both can injure hands and damage the movement, and both are managed by letting power down before any work begins.

Mechanism

A mainspring stores a large amount of energy in its barrel, and if it is released suddenly it can spin the barrel, break teeth, and cut hands. Weights, typically several kilograms each on a longcase clock, hang on lines or chains, and if a line breaks or a weight is lifted carelessly, the weight falls and the case is damaged. Safe handling means removing weights first, supporting them as they come down, and letting a mainspring down in small, controlled steps with a let-down tool, never by hand alone.

Maintenance

Never open a movement with the power on, never let a mainspring down by holding the barrel by hand, and never stand under a weight as it is removed. Wear eye protection when working on a mainspring barrel, and keep hands clear of the barrel's path.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration workshop keeps a let-down tool, a mainspring winder, and a weight cradle, and it trains every worker in power let-down before they touch a movement. Record the power state, weights removed or spring let down, on the job card before stripping begins.

Tools

Let-down tool, mainspring winder, weight cradle, eye protection, and gloves.

title: Servicing a Weight-Driven Movement
body:
Specifications

A weight-driven longcase movement is powered by weights hanging on lines or chains, driving the going train through a barrel or a gut line drum. An eight-day movement runs for eight days on one winding, and a thirty-hour movement runs for about thirty hours, and the difference is in the barrel size and the gearing, not in the escapement.

Mechanism

Winding raises the weights, and as they fall they turn the barrel, which drives the centre wheel and the rest of the going train. The lines or chains must run true on their drums and pulleys, and the weights must hang free without touching the case or each other. The strike and chime trains have their own weights on a triple-weight clock, and each weight must be matched to its train.

Maintenance

Check the lines or chains for fraying at every service, and replace a frayed line before it breaks, because a falling weight damages the case and the movement. Keep the pulleys clean and oiled, and never swap the weights between trains, because the going, strike, and chime trains need different weights.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration weight service replaces worn lines with the correct gut or cable, checks the drums for grooves, and matches each weight to its train by the maker's marks or by testing. Test the run time for a full week after service.

Tools

Gut lines or cable, pulleys, weight scale, screwdrivers, and clock oil.

title: Handling a Mainspring Safely
body:
Specifications

A mainspring is a coiled spring in a barrel that powers a spring-driven clock, and it is the most dangerous part of the movement to handle. It must be let down, removed, cleaned, and rewound with tools made for the job, never by hand alone.

Mechanism

The spring is wound in its barrel, and its energy drives the barrel's teeth, which drive the going train. Letting it down means holding the barrel with a let-down tool and releasing the click a fraction at a time, so the spring unwinds slowly. Removing it means opening the barrel and lifting the spring out with a winder, and rewinding means winding it back into the barrel with the same tool, keeping the spring's coils even.

Maintenance

Never let a mainspring down by hand, never open a barrel without holding the spring, and never reuse a spring with a cracked or set coil, because it will break in service and damage the train. Wear eye protection for all mainspring work.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration mainspring service checks the spring for set, cracks, and rust, replaces a faulty spring with one of the same strength and size, and records the spring's dimensions in the service notes. Test the power at the escape wheel after fitting, before closing the movement.

Tools

Let-down tool, mainspring winder, barrel opener, eye protection, and gloves.

title: Regulating a Pendulum Clock
body:
Specifications

Regulating means adjusting the pendulum's effective length so the clock keeps correct time, using the rating nut under the pendulum bob. Raising the bob shortens the pendulum and makes the clock run faster, and lowering the bob lengthens it and makes the clock run slower.

Mechanism

The rating nut turns on a threaded rod under the bob, and one full turn typically changes the rate by about ten seconds a day on a seconds pendulum, though the exact figure varies by movement. Regulation is done in small steps, with the clock's rate measured over at least a day between steps, because a single hour's measurement is too noisy to trust.

Maintenance

Regulate only after the clock is clean, oiled, in beat, and level, because regulating a dirty or out-of-beat clock chases a moving target. Never turn the rating nut by large amounts at once, and never regulate by bending the pendulum rod.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration regulation records the rate before and after each nut turn, and it checks the rate at the same time of day, because temperature changes the pendulum's length and the rate with it. A clock that gains in summer and loses in winter usually needs a temperature-compensated pendulum, not more regulation.

Tools

Rating nut tool, timing machine, and a rate log.

title: Caring for a Dial and Hands
body:
Specifications

Dial care means cleaning and protecting the painted or silvered dial and the hands, without damaging the paint, the numerals, or the hand fittings. Longcase dials are often painted on iron or brass, with applied spandrels and a subsidiary seconds dial, and their paint is fragile once it has aged.

Mechanism

The dial is cleaned with a soft, dry brush, and only very gently, because paint flakes if it is rubbed or wetted. Hands are cleaned separately, with a soft cloth, and refitted with their collets square and their clearance set so they do not touch each other or the dial. The hands must be set so the hour hand points correctly at each hour, which is checked by the strike: the clock should strike the hour the hands show.

Maintenance

Never use water or cleaner on a painted dial, never bend a hand to correct a strike error, and never polish a silvered dial with abrasive, because the silvering is thin and will wear through. A dial with flaking paint should be left alone and shown to a specialist, not cleaned harder.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration dial repair consolidates flaking paint, retouches only where the loss is certain, and matches the original colours, so the dial keeps its age. Record the dial's condition with photographs before any work.

Tools

Soft brushes, hand puller, hand setter, loupe, and camera.

title: Troubleshooting a Strike and Chime Train
body:
Specifications

Strike and chime troubleshooting means finding why a clock strikes the wrong hour, strikes at the wrong time, or does not chime, by testing each train in order. The fault is usually in the warning, the locking, the rack or count wheel, or the chime barrel position, not in the going train.

Mechanism

Test the going train first, then the strike train alone, then the chime train alone, counting the blows at every hour. A strike that counts correctly at three but fails at twelve points to a worn snail step or a worn count-wheel notch at twelve. A chime that plays the wrong quarter points to a barrel one step out or a selector fault. A strike that lags points to a warning fault.

Maintenance

Never bend a rack, a count wheel, or a selector lever to cure a fault without finding the worn part first, because bending hides the fault and creates a new one. Never adjust the hands to correct a strike count on a rack-and-snail clock, because the snail is driven by the hands and the count will follow the hands.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration troubleshooting records the fault at every hour, the train that was at fault, and the part replaced or adjusted, so the next service can see the history. Test the full twelve hours, twice, before returning the clock.

Tools

Counting chart, warning lever gauge, screwdrivers, and a beat tester.

title: Polishing Pivots
body:
Specifications

Pivot polishing means smoothing a pivot that has become rough or grooved, so it runs freely in its hole with fresh oil. Pivots roughen because they turn in their holes for decades under load, and a rough pivot drags, loses power, and makes the clock run unevenly.

Mechanism

The pivot is held in a lathe or a pivot polisher and smoothed with a fine file, then with a burnisher, which hardens and polishes the surface without removing much metal. The pivot must stay round and straight, and its diameter must not be reduced by more than a few hundredths of a millimetre, or it will be loose in its hole and need bushing.

Maintenance

Never polish a pivot with coarse abrasive, never polish a pivot that is already undersize, and never polish a pivot without checking its hole, because a polished pivot in a worn hole still runs badly. Check the pivot for straightness before and after polishing.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration pivot polish records the pivot's diameter before and after, and it checks the depthing after polishing, because a thinner pivot sits differently in its hole. Test the wheel for freedom before oiling.

Tools

Pivot polisher, fine files, burnisher, micrometer, and loupe.

title: Checking Wear: Depthing and Endshake
body:
Specifications

Depthing and endshake checks measure whether wheels mesh correctly and whether they have the right freedom along their arbors. Depthing is the distance between two wheel centres, which sets how deeply their teeth mesh, and endshake is the small freedom a wheel has to move along its arbor between the plates.

Mechanism

Depthing is checked with a depthing tool, which holds the two wheels at their correct centres and shows whether the teeth mesh too deeply, too shallowly, or correctly. Endshake is checked by lifting each wheel along its arbor and feeling the small movement, which should be present but not excessive. Too little endshake binds the wheel, and too much lets it wander and wear its pivots unevenly.

Maintenance

Check depthing and endshake after any bushing or pivot work, because both change the wheel's position. Never close the plates without checking every wheel pair, because a depthing fault found after closing means stripping the movement again.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration inspection records the depthing and endshake of every wheel pair, and it corrects faults by bushing, pivot work, or plate work, in that order. Test the movement for freedom before oiling.

Tools

Depthing tool, endshake gauge, loupe, and service notes.

title: Reassembling and Testing in Beat
body:
Specifications

Reassembly means putting the cleaned movement back together, checking every wheel for freedom, setting the beat, and testing the movement on a stand before it goes back into its case. It is the last step of a service, and it is where a service succeeds or fails.

Mechanism

The wheels are fitted in order, the plates are closed, and each wheel is checked for freedom by turning it by hand. The escapement is fitted, the beat is set, and the movement is run on a test stand for at least a week, with its rate, beat, and strike counted daily. Only when the movement runs steadily for a week is it returned to its case and its pendulum fitted.

Maintenance

Never return a movement to its case after a bench test of an hour, because faults in rate and strike show over days, not hours. Never fit the pendulum before the beat is set, because the pendulum's weight hides a beat fault.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration reassembly records the test week's rate and beat daily, and it notes any adjustment made during the week, so the owner can see the movement's true performance. Test the strike at every hour during the test week.

Tools

Test stand, beat tester, timing machine, and a rate log.

title: Long-Term Storage and Environment
body:
Specifications

Long-term storage means keeping a clock safe when it is not running, and environment means the room it lives in: its temperature, humidity, light, and level. Clocks suffer more from damp, sunlight, and dust than from running, and a clock stored badly can be damaged in a year.

Mechanism

A clock in storage should have its weights removed, its pendulum removed and packed separately, its movement covered against dust, and its case kept upright, level, and out of direct sunlight. The room should be dry, with stable temperature, because damp rusts pivots and swells wood, and heat dries wood and cracks veneer. A running clock should also stand level, out of sunlight, and away from radiators, because a leaning clock runs out of beat and a hot clock runs fast as its pendulum expands.

Maintenance

Never store a clock with its weights hanging, never lay a longcase clock on its side with its movement in place, and never store a clock in a damp garage or attic. Check a stored clock every few months for damp and dust, and wind a stored spring-driven clock occasionally so its spring does not set.

Build and restoration guidance

A restoration storage plan records the clock's condition when stored, the weights and pendulum removed, and the room's conditions, so the clock can be returned to service with a known history. Inspect the movement before running a clock that has been stored for a year or more.

Tools

Dust covers, weight cradle, pendulum packing, hygrometer, and a spirit level.
